passage:
In March I missed the deadline for a client's tax filing at our accounts firm. It cost them a late fee, and it was my fault; I'd let it slide under other work. After that I stayed until ten every night for five weeks. I rechecked every file twice. When Lalit, my team lead, offered to split my load, I said "No, I've got it," too quickly. I skipped lunch, then weekends. I think I was trying to pay it off, like a fine, with my evenings.
In week six I fell asleep at my desk and woke with the keyboard printed on my cheek. Lalit sat me down. "Chaitanya, you made one mistake. You told the client. We fixed the process. It's done. Working yourself sick doesn't make it more done."
I cried a little, embarrassingly. Then I went home at six.

qa.q: For how long did Chaitanya stay until ten every night?
qa.a: Five weeks.

qa.q: Why did Chaitanya refuse Lalit's offer to split the load?
qa.a: Chaitanya felt so guilty about the missed deadline that it had to be paid off personally, like a fine, and accepting help would have felt like not suffering enough.

qa.q: What turning point helped Chaitanya stop the penance?
qa.a: Falling asleep at the desk, and Lalit pointing out that the mistake was owned, told and fixed, so extra suffering added nothing.

qa.q: How might Lalit have felt watching Chaitanya refuse help for weeks?
qa.a: Worried and a bit helpless, seeing a capable colleague wear down over something already settled.

grounding: An employee who missed a deadline works late for weeks and refuses help as penance, until a team lead points out the mistake is already owned and fixed.

subtype: Overworking to make up for a mistake [Actor]
passage:
Supervisor's note, 18 July
Mahima, one of our junior nurses, gave a patient's evening medicine late on 2 July. The patient was not harmed, it was reported properly, and we reviewed the handover process. It was a gap in the system as much as a personal one.
Since then Mahima has taken extra shifts every week, comes in early, stays late, and has refused every offer of help, including mine. Yesterday she was restocking supplies at 11 p.m. on her day off. She looks exhausted and has lost her usual laugh.
Today I spoke to her. I said the mistake was real, she owned it well, and the matter is closed. Extra shifts don't undo it; they only wear her down. We agreed: no extra shifts for a month, and a chat with the staff counsellor if the guilt keeps sitting heavy.
Sharmila Nair, Ward Supervisor

qa.q: When was Mahima restocking supplies on her day off?
qa.a: At 11 p.m.

qa.q: Why might Mahima refuse every offer of help?
qa.a: Her guilt about the late medicine seems to make her feel she must make up for it alone, as if accepting help would cancel her penance.

qa.q: Which choice in Sharmila's note is most useful, and why?
qa.a: Clearly closing the matter and setting no extra shifts for a month, with the counsellor as backup, because it replaces exhausting penance with ownership that is already done.

qa.q: How might Mahima's colleagues see her extra shifts?
qa.a: They may admire her dedication but worry about her tiredness and her missing laugh.

grounding: A ward supervisor notes a young nurse overworking and refusing help after a mistake, and closes the matter so the guilt stops costing her so much.

Wednesday, 11:40 p.m.
Another late night at the design studio. Third week in a row. Ever since I sent the client the wrong version of the brochure and they printed 500 copies, I've been trying to fix it by working harder than anyone. I redid three other projects nobody asked me to redo. Arnab offered to take the Kumar account off my plate, and I nearly bit his head off. "I'll manage."
Tonight on the bus I did the maths: about sixty extra hours. The brochure mistake took maybe ten minutes. I'm paying for a ten-minute mistake with sixty hours, and nobody even asked me to.
What I haven't done is sit with my boss and say plainly, "I made this error, and here's how I'll prevent it." That would take fifteen minutes. Tomorrow. Fifteen minutes. Then home by seven.
Gopika

passage:
In the panchayat office at Kherwadi, Sarita, twenty-five, had missed the deadline to send the updated ration list to the block office. Eleven families waited an extra week for their grain. Nobody shouted. The block officer simply gave a new date.
But since then Sarita had stayed after dark every evening, rechecking lists that were already correct, sweeping the office herself, typing up records nobody had asked for. When Lata, who shared her desk, offered to take the pension files, Sarita snapped, "No. I'll do it. It's my mess."
On the last bus home she fell asleep against the window and missed her stop.
The next morning Lata put a cup of tea on her desk. "You've paid for that week ten times over. Why not just tell the sarpanch what went wrong and what you'll do next time? Then let me help."
Sarita stared at the tea. It sounded almost too simple.

qa.a: Eleven families.

qa.a: Her guilt over the missed deadline made accepting help feel like cheating; doing everything alone felt like the only way to make up for it.

qa.a: Telling the sarpanch once what went wrong and what she'll change, then letting Lata share the files, which would cost far less than weeks of late nights.

passage: Sarita, you've stayed till eleven every night this month because of that one late report? Come, let your Sharmila didi tell you something. When I was twenty-four, at the insurance office in Nagpur, I missed a client deadline by two days. Just once. The client was annoyed, my manager was annoyed, and I felt like the worst person alive. So I decided to make up for it. I came in at seven and left at midnight for six weeks. Colleagues offered help; I said no, it was my mess. I got thin. I snapped at my mother. One day my manager, a quiet woman, called me into her room. "Sharmila, I forgave the deadline in a week. Why haven't you?" I burst into tears. Then she said, "Just say it was your mistake, fix the process, and go home." That was the turning point. I did.

qa.a: Six weeks.

qa.a: She felt guilty and ashamed, believing she had to pay for the mistake herself, as if hard work could erase it.

qa.a: Her manager asking why she hadn't forgiven herself and suggesting simple ownership, which ended the exhausting penance.

qa.q: How might the manager have felt watching Sharmila work until midnight?
qa.a: The manager probably felt concerned and sad, having forgiven the deadline weeks earlier.

grounding: Illustrates, through an elder's memory, an employee overworking for weeks to erase a missed deadline, and learning simple ownership costs less.
